subject: Geography
name: Geography, Year 11
about: HSC, Natural systems, people and environments
syllabus: NSW Geography 11-12 Syllabus (2022), Year 11 focus areas

points.title: Place and space
points.brief: Place is a part of the Earth's surface with its own meaning to people. Space is how things are arranged and spread across the surface.

points.title: Environment and interconnection
points.brief: The environment is the living and non-living world around us. Interconnection is how people, places and processes affect each other.

points.title: Scale
points.brief: Geographers look at issues at local, regional, national and global scales, and an explanation at one scale may differ at another.

points.title: Change over time
points.brief: Places and environments change over different time spans, from a flood in a day to climate change over centuries.

points.title: The atmosphere
points.brief: The layer of gases around the Earth, which holds weather and climate and keeps the planet warm through the greenhouse effect.

points.title: The hydrosphere
points.brief: All the Earth's water, in oceans, rivers, lakes, ice and groundwater, moved around by the water cycle.

points.title: The lithosphere
points.brief: The Earth's crust and upper mantle, the rocks and landforms that make the surface.

points.title: The biosphere
points.brief: All living things and the places they live, which depend on the other three spheres.

points.title: How the spheres interact
points.brief: Energy and matter flow between the spheres, so a change in one, such as a volcanic eruption, affects the others.

points.title: Plate tectonics
points.brief: The lithosphere is broken into plates that move slowly. Where they meet they cause earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building.

points.title: Weathering and erosion
points.brief: Weathering breaks rock down in place. Erosion carries the pieces away by water, wind and ice, shaping landforms.

points.title: The water cycle
points.brief: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation and flows back to the sea over land and underground.

points.title: Atmospheric circulation and climate
points.brief: Uneven heating by the sun drives winds and pressure belts, which, with ocean currents, set the world's climate zones.

points.title: Natural hazards
points.brief: Events such as bushfires, floods, cyclones and droughts are natural processes that become hazards when they affect people.

points.title: Population distribution and density
points.brief: Where people live and how crowded places are. People cluster near water, fertile land, jobs and good climates.

points.title: Population change
points.brief: Population grows or shrinks through births, deaths and migration.

points.title: The demographic transition model
points.brief: As countries develop, death rates fall first and birth rates later, so population grows fast before it levels off.

points.title: Migration
points.brief: People move for push factors, such as war or poverty, and pull factors, such as jobs and safety, within and between countries.

points.title: Urbanisation
points.brief: The growing share of people living in cities. More than half the world's people now live in urban areas.

points.title: Patterns of development
points.brief: Income, health and education differ greatly between and within countries, measured by indicators such as GDP per person and the Human Development Index.

points.title: Economic activity and location
points.brief: Industries locate near resources, markets, transport and workers, and these patterns shift as technology changes.

points.title: Globalisation and flows
points.brief: Goods, money, people and ideas move faster and further than ever, linking distant places.

points.title: Cultural diffusion
points.brief: Ideas, languages and cultural practices spread between places through trade, migration and media.

points.title: Human impacts on natural systems
points.brief: Clearing land, farming, mining and building change natural systems, from soils and rivers to the climate.

points.title: Land degradation
points.brief: Soil erosion, salinity and loss of vegetation reduce the land's ability to support plants, animals and people.

points.title: Managing water
points.brief: Dams, irrigation and water trading support farming and cities but change rivers. The Murray-Darling Basin shows the competing demands.

points.title: Renewable and non-renewable resources
points.brief: Renewable resources, such as sunlight and forests, can be replaced. Non-renewable ones, such as coal, run out once used.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander care for Country
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for Country for tens of thousands of years, and their knowledge now informs land and fire management.

points.title: Sustainable management
points.brief: Using resources in ways that meet present needs without harming future generations, balancing social, economic and environmental goals.

points.title: The inquiry process
points.brief: Asking a geographical question, gathering and processing information, analysing it and drawing conclusions that answer the question.

points.title: Fieldwork and primary data
points.brief: Collecting data first-hand through observations, measurements, surveys and interviews.

points.title: Secondary data
points.brief: Using data already collected by others, such as census figures, climate records and reports, and checking how reliable it is.

points.title: Maps and spatial technologies
points.brief: Topographic maps, satellite images and geographic information systems (GIS) show and analyse where things are.

points.title: Presenting findings
points.brief: Communicating results with maps, graphs, photographs and a clear written report.
